title: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
hook: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tulsidas bowed to the saints, to the wicked, and to the whole world as full of Sita and Ram, and the swan took the milk from the water. Where did you find the milk in the mixture? Day nine hundred twenty-six.

A truck driver in traffic, murmuring under his breath. A student outside an exam hall, lips moving. A grandmother on a Tuesday evening, a small book open on her lap that she doesn't need to read because she knows every word. They could all be saying the same thing: a hymn to Hanuman, short enough to say in a few minutes, steady enough to lean on. Tradition gives it to Tulsidas, and the hymn signs his name near its end. Today we walk into it, verse by verse, from the first line.
screen: `MURMURED IN TRAFFIC.` → `KNOWN BY HEART.` → `THE HANUMAN CHALISA.`

segments.voice: The Chalisa doesn't start with Hanuman. It starts with a mirror. The first couplet says, roughly: with the dust from my teacher's lotus feet I polish the mirror of my mind, and then I sing the pure fame of Ram. Before praising anyone, clean the glass, so what you see isn't smudged by you. The second couplet is even more honest. Knowing myself to be without understanding, it says, I remember Hanuman, son of the wind. Give me strength, wisdom and knowledge, and take away my troubles. That's the posture of the whole hymn. Not I am strong. I'm not wise enough, so I'm calling on the one who is. Then the verses proper begin: victory to Hanuman, ocean of knowledge and virtue. And they go on to praise him piece by piece. His strength. His speed. His leap across the sea. The way he brought the healing herb that revived Lakshman. But listen for the line that says what all that strength is for. Hanuman, in the Chalisa, is the guard at Ram's door. All that power, and it's used for service, near Ram, doing what's needed. And near the end, the poet steps forward and gives his own name. Tulsidas, the hymn says, is forever Hari's servant, and he asks the Lord to make a home in his heart. So the man who once crossed a flooded river for his wife ends up describing himself the way he describes Hanuman: a servant. The strength the hymn asks for is a servant's strength, a strength that stands at the door.
screen: `POLISH THE MIRROR OF THE MIND.` · `WITHOUT UNDERSTANDING, I REMEMBER.` · `THE GUARD AT RAM'S DOOR.` · then, large: `TULSIDAS, FOREVER HARI'S SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Start where the hymn starts: with a mirror. Picture your mind as a glass with the day's smudges on it, a worry, a grudge, a hurry. Don't scrub. Just breathe on it, and with each breath out, let one smudge soften. Then, if it feels honest, admit one thing you don't understand right now, in your life or in the world. And ask, quietly, for the strength to serve anyway. If you pray, you can turn that asking to God, or to Hanuman, in whatever words you already use. The bell holds the time.
Tulsidas. The poet of Ram, to whom tradition gives the Hanuman Chalisa, the hymn that cleans the mirror of the mind and ends by calling Tulsidas forever Hari's servant.
Your line: polish the mirror. Today, before you judge something, polish the mirror for one breath. Day nine hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Devotees of Hanuman recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often from memory, at home and in temples, and some make a point of saying it on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

fork.reveal: it starts with a mirror: clean the mind with the dust of the teacher's feet, then sing. then it admits it lacks understanding.

trapdoor: what you thought: a song asking a strong god for strength.
what it means: a hymn that begins by cleaning the mirror and admitting it doesn't understand, then praises strength used for service.
what a scholar hears: the hymn signs itself, calling Tulsidas forever Hari's servant, so the poet ends in Hanuman's own posture.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the opening couplets (polishing the mirror of the mind with the dust of the guru's feet; buddhi hin tanu janike, asking for bal, buddhi, vidya) and the verses cited (jai hanuman gyan gun sagar; ram duare tum rakhvare; tulsidas sada hari chera, kije nath hriday mah dera).
Authorship is framed as 'tradition gives it to Tulsidas' plus the hymn's own signature line; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with that.
The meaning of 'chalisa' and the count of verses are deliberately not stated, under the claims rule.
The hook's everyday scenes (driver, student, grandmother) are illustrative, not claims about practice; howItsDone mentions Tuesdays and Saturdays with 'some'. Confirm.
'Brought the healing herb that revived Lakshman' paraphrases laye sajivan lakhan jiyaye; confirm.
Day 927's review (Surdas, already on disk) calls the Chalisa 'a servant's song about strength'; this script ends there to match.

Editor pass: 'at the very end' and the match pair 'the last verse' corrected to 'near the end' (the signature chaupai is followed by a closing doha, and the hook already said 'near its end'); cut 'he doesn't want the throne', which the Chalisa does not say; 'the word that keeps him in his place' reworded so it no longer sounds diminishing.
